Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. On a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, a **continuous-time filtration** is a family
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ such that
$\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_t$ whenever $0\le s\le t$. A process
$X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** when $X_t$ is measurable from
$(\Omega,\mathcal F_t)$ to its state space at every $t$.

For any process of random elements $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$, its **natural
filtration** is

$$\mathcal F_t^X=\sigma\!\left(\{X_u^{-1}(C):0\le u\le t,\ C\text{ measurable in the state space of }X_u\}\right).$$

The generated sigma-algebra exists by
[[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]]. Its generator families
are nested in $t$, so $(\mathcal F_t^X)_{t\ge0}$ is a filtration; every
$X_t$ is $\mathcal F_t^X$-measurable, and minimality makes this the smallest
filtration to which $X$ is adapted. No completion or right-continuous
augmentation is included.

A real process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is an **all-pairs continuous-time
martingale** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when:

1. $M$ is adapted;
2. $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$; and
3. for every $0\le s\le t$,
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$

The equality in clause 3 is equality of the almost-everywhere classes in
[[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]. At $s=t$ it is the
known-variable identity. The word “continuous-time” specifies the index set;
it does not assert path continuity. Likewise the definition imposes neither
right continuity nor completeness on the filtration. AC is declared exactly
because the library's conditional-expectation existence theorem uses it; the
filtration, adaptation, and natural-filtration constructions make no choices.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a set. The **counting set function** on $\mathcal P(X)$ is

$$\#_X(E):=\begin{cases}|E|,&E\text{ is finite},\\+\infty,&E\text{ is infinite},\end{cases}$$

where finite means equinumerous with a natural number ([[def-countable]]) and $+\infty$ belongs to the extended real line ([[def-extended-reals]]). The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a measure, and hence deserves the name **counting measure**, is proved in [[prop-counting-measure-is-a-measure]].

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim: Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $G$ be an abelian group written additively ([[def-group]]) and let
$\phi:G\to\mathbb C$ be a function ([[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]).
Then $\phi$ is **positive definite** when for every integer $n\ge0$, every
finite family $x_1,\dots,x_n\in G$ and all coefficients
$c_1,\dots,c_n\in\mathbb C$ one has
$$\sum_{j=1}^{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}c_j\overline{c_k}\,\phi(x_j-x_k)\ \ge\ 0 .$$
The sum for $n=0$ is the empty sum $0$, so the convention covers it; repeated
points $x_j=x_k$ are allowed, so the finite matrices tested are the Hermitian
matrices $[\phi(x_j-x_k)]_{j,k}$. No continuity, boundedness or measurability
is part of the definition.

**Elementary consequences.** The claims below are immediate from the defining
inequality and are recorded here for later use. Taking $n=1$, $x_1=0$ and
$c_1=1$ gives $\phi(0)\ge0$. Taking $n=2$, $x_1=0$, $x_2=x$ and
$c_1=1$, $c_2=t$ gives
$$(1+|t|^2)\phi(0)+\overline{t}\,\phi(-x)+t\,\phi(x)\ \ge\ 0\qquad\text{for every }t\in\mathbb C .$$
The left side is real and equal to its own conjugate for every $t$, so
comparing coefficients at $t=1$ and $t=i$ gives $\phi(-x)=\overline{\phi(x)}$
([[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]); hence every tested matrix is
Hermitian. If $\phi(x)\ne0$, choose $t=-\overline{\phi(x)}/|\phi(x)|$, so $|t|=1$ and $t\phi(x)=-|\phi(x)|$. The inequality becomes $2\phi(0)-2|\phi(x)|\ge0$, hence $|\phi(x)|\le\phi(0)$; if $\phi(x)=0$, the same bound follows from $\phi(0)\ge0$. Thus a positive definite $\phi$ satisfies
$\phi(0)\ge0$, $\phi(x)=\overline{\phi(-x)}$ and $|\phi(x)|\le\phi(0)$ for all
$x\in G$.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume AC on a fixed probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. A **rowwise square-integrable martingale-difference array** consists of families $(\mathcal F_{n,k})_{n\ge1,k\ge0}$ and $(Z_{n,k})_{n,k\ge1}$ such that for each $n$ the $\mathcal F_{n,k}$ form an increasing filtration of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\mathcal F$, $Z_{n,k}\in L^2$ is $\mathcal F_{n,k}$-measurable, and
$$\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}\mid\mathcal F_{n,k-1}]=0\quad\text{a.s.}$$
Define
$$M_{n,m}=\sum_{k=1}^mZ_{n,k},\qquad v_{n,k}=\mathbb E[Z_{n,k}^2\mid\mathcal F_{n,k-1}],\qquad \Gamma_{n,m}=\sum_{k=1}^m v_{n,k}.$$
Each $v_{n,k}$ is nonnegative, integrable, and $\mathcal F_{n,k-1}$-measurable; hence $\Gamma_{n,m}$ is an increasing predictable **variance clock**, while $M_{n,m}$ is a rowwise $L^2$ martingale. A finite triangular row is included by putting $Z_{n,k}=0$ and holding the filtration fixed after its last column. This preserves both limiting sums. AC is used only through conditional-moment existence and countable representative selection.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $S\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ with Borel sigma-algebra $\mathcal E$, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a
probability space, and let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a stochastic process with each
$Y_n:\Omega\to S$ a random element
([[def-stochastic-process-and-finite-dimensional-distributions]]). The process
$Y$ is **strictly stationary** when every finite-dimensional law is unchanged
by a common nonnegative time shift: for every $r\ge1$, every
$0\le n_1<\cdots<n_r$ and every $m\ge0$,

$$\mathcal L(Y_{m+n_1},\ldots,Y_{m+n_r})=\mathcal L(Y_{n_1},\ldots,Y_{n_r}).$$

The **canonical path law** of $Y$ is the pushforward
$\mathbb P_Y=\mathcal L(Y)$ of $\mathbb P$ under the coordinate map
$\omega\mapsto(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$, a probability measure on the product
space $S^{\mathbb N_0}$ with its product sigma-algebra. The **left shift** is
$\theta(z)_n=z_{n+1}$ for $z=(z_n)_{n\ge0}\in S^{\mathbb N_0}$.

A strictly stationary process is called **ergodic** when the canonical shift $\theta$ is ergodic
for $\mathbb P_Y$ in the sense of
[[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]. The shift-invariance needed for that
definition, namely that $\theta$ is measure preserving for $\mathbb P_Y$, is
proved below for strictly stationary $Y$, so in that case
$(S^{\mathbb N_0},\mathcal E^{\otimes\mathbb N_0},\mathbb P_Y,\theta)$ is a
probability measure-preserving system in the sense of
[[def-measure-preserving-transformation-and-system]].

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $K$ be a probability kernel on $(E,\mathcal E)$,
let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\ge0})$ be a filtered
probability space, and let $X=(X_n)_{n\ge0}$ be an adapted $E$-valued process.
We call $X$ a **time-homogeneous Markov chain with transition kernel $K$ relative
to $(\mathcal F_n)$** if, for every $n\ge0$ and $A\in\mathcal E$,
$$ \mathbb P(X_{n+1}\in A\mid\mathcal F_n)=K(X_n,A)\qquad\text{a.s.} $$
Here the left side is an almost-everywhere class of conditional-probability
versions. The right side is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable because
$x\mapsto K(x,A)$ is $\mathcal E$-measurable and $X_n$ is
$\mathcal F_n/\mathcal E$-measurable.

If $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_0,\ldots,X_n)$, we say simply that $X$ is a Markov
chain relative to its **natural filtration**. A chain relative to a larger
filtration is therefore a stronger assertion, not merely a change of notation.

Choice is used only through the library construction that supplies conditional
expectations, hence conditional probabilities, simultaneously as
almost-everywhere classes; this definition asserts no pointwise regular
conditional distribution.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let
$F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing and right-continuous, and let
$\mu_F$ be its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure. Then for every $a < b$,

$$\mu_F((a,b)) = F(b^-) - F(a),$$

$$\mu_F([a,b]) = F(b) - F(a^-),$$

$$\mu_F([a,b)) = F(b^-) - F(a^-),$$

and

$$\mu_F(\{a\}) = F(a) - F(a^-).$$

Consequently $a$ is an atom of $\mu_F$ in the sense of
[[def-atom-of-a-measure-on-r]] if and only if $F(a) > F(a^-)$, and the set of
atoms of $\mu_F$ is at most countable.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim: Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X,Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be square-integrable real random variables on one
probability space, and write
$$W:=\operatorname{span}\big([1],[Y_1],\dots,[Y_n]\big)\subseteq L^2(\mathbb P),$$
where $[\cdot]$ denotes the almost-everywhere class from
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]].

Then there is a unique class $[Z_*]\in W$ minimizing $\|[X]-[Z]\|_2$ over
$[Z]\in W$. This minimizing class has an affine representative
$Z_*=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^n a_jY_j$, and its coefficients satisfy
$$a_0=\mathbb E[X]-\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\mathbb E[Y_j],$$
$$\sum_{j=1}^n \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)a_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y_i)\qquad(1\le i\le n).$$

The class $[Z_*]$ is unique. If the covariance matrix
$\Gamma=(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j))_{i,j}$ is singular, the coefficient vector
need not be uniquely determined by the normal equations, but any two solutions
yield the same predictor almost surely.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume AC. If $M$ is a martingale and $\sigma\le\tau$ are stopping times bounded by a deterministic $N$, then
$$\mathbb E[M_\tau\mid\mathcal F_\sigma]=M_\sigma\quad\text{a.s.},$$
so $\mathbb EM_\tau=\mathbb EM_\sigma$. For a submartingale $X$ the conditional and expectation inequalities point upward; for a supermartingale they point downward.

Every invertible matrix $A\in M_n(\mathbb F)$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, has a unique factorisation

$$A=QR,$$

where $Q^*Q=I$ and $R$ is upper triangular with positive real diagonal entries. Thus $Q$ is orthogonal over $\mathbb R$ and unitary over $\mathbb C$. The assertion includes the unique $0\times0$ factorisation.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

items.reusable_clause_exact: A.s./L1 averages under strict stationarity, integrability and AC; only ergodicity makes the limit constant. No dependent-data CLT or weak-stationarity definition.
items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume AC ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $Y=(Y_n)_{n\ge0}$ be a real-valued
strictly stationary process with $\mathbb E|Y_0|<\infty$
([[def-stationary-process-and-canonical-shift]]), with canonical path law
$\mathbb P_Y$ and left shift $\theta$. Let
$\mathcal I=\{A:\theta^{-1}A=A\}$ be the strictly invariant sigma-algebra on
path space ([[def-strict-and-mod-null-invariant-sigma-algebras]]). Then

$$\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}Y_k\ \longrightarrow\ \mathbb E_{\mathbb P_Y}[z_0\mid\mathcal I]\circ\Phi \qquad\text{almost surely and in }L^1(\mathbb P),$$

where $\Phi(\omega)=(Y_n(\omega))_{n\ge0}$ and the conditional expectation is
that of [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. If moreover the
canonical shift is ergodic ([[def-ergodic-measure-preserving-system]]), then
the limit is the constant $\mathbb EY_0$. For complex-valued processes the
assertions hold componentwise for real and imaginary parts.

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

items.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element. Its
**law** or **distribution** is the set function
$$\mathbb P_X:\Sigma\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \mathbb P_X(B):=\mathbb P(X^{-1}(B)).$$

Thus the law of $X$ records the probability of each measurable target set by
pulling it back to an event in the original probability space.

findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** fixed-design-linear-regression-and-estimability / fixed-design-linear-regression-and-estimability-examples. **A:** For fixed $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$ and $Y=X\beta+\epsilon$, define least-squares estimators as $\arg\min_b\|Y-Xb\|_2^2$. The fitted vector $P_{\operatorname{col}X}Y$ and residual are unique; coefficient minimizers form $\hat\beta+\ker X$. A linear contrast $c^T\beta$ is estimable iff $c\in\operatorname{row}(X)$, equivalently $c=X^Ta$ for some $a$ so that $a^TY$ is unbiased under $E\epsilon=0$. For full-column-rank $X$, $\hat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^TY$. Under fixed full-rank $X$, $E\epsilon=0$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon)=\sigma^2I_n$ with $\sigma^2>0$, prove OLS is BLUE for estimable contrasts; Gaussianity is not needed. **Proof:** use the published least-squares normal equation, then write any linear unbiased contrast estimate as $a^TY$, $X^Ta=c$, and cancel the covariance cross-term against the OLS representative. **B:** collinearity, estimable contrast, heteroskedasticity, leverage/diagnostics. **Requires:** SME-01; MSF-01/02; thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation, thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point, thm-rank-nullity, and the published first/second-moment identities. **Sources:** MIT 18.443 regression pp. 1–4; Wickham pp. 2–6, proof pp. 5–6; diagnostics pp. 8, 11–12, 17.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** exact-gaussian-linear-regression-inference / exact-gaussian-linear-regression-inference-examples. **A:** Fixed full-column-rank $X\in\mathbb R^{n\times p}$, $1\le p<n$, and $\epsilon\sim N_n(0,\sigma^2I_n)$, $\sigma^2>0$. pairs.title: Generalized linear models and Fisher scoring
findings_and_repairs: Corrected the GLM IRLS scale to the common dispersion scale and retained the deviance diagnostic source gap.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** generalized-linear-models-and-fisher-scoring / generalized-linear-models-and-fisher-scoring-examples. **A:** For independent $Y_i$ under a stated product sampling law, define exponential-family density/mass $f_i(y;\theta_i,\phi)=\exp\{(y\theta_i-b(\theta_i))/a_i(\phi)+c_i(y,\phi)\}$ relative to its base measure; state common-dispersion restrictions when used. Define $\mu_i=b'(\theta_i)$, variance $a_i(\phi)b''(\theta_i)$, link $g(\mu_i)=\eta_i=x_i^T\beta$, and canonical link $\theta_i=\eta_i$. Under common scale $a(\phi)>0$, the canonical score is $X^T(y-\mu)/a(\phi)$ and Hessian is $-X^T\operatorname{diag}(b''(\eta_i))X/a(\phi)$; strictly positive $b''(\eta_i)$ and full column rank make $\ell$ strictly concave, yielding at most one finite stationary maximizer, not existence. Define Fisher scoring/IRLS at finite $\beta$: $z_i=\eta_i+(y_i-\mu_i)/(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)$, $w_i=(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)^2/\{a(\phi)V(\mu_i)\}>0$, and output a weighted least-squares minimizer; prove this equals the Fisher-scoring step when information is invertible. No termination/global-convergence guarantee. Define deviance $D=2\{\sup_{\beta\in\Theta_{\rm sat}}\ell(\beta)-\sup_{\beta\in\Theta_{\rm fit}}\ell(\beta)\}$ only for nested stated models on common support, so it is nonnegative by set inclusion; no residual distribution or goodness-of-fit reference law is claimed. Score/information identities require common support, differentiability and integrable derivative envelopes. MSF-15 applies only to a matching fixed-dimensional iid random-design model with its exact interior/regularity assumptions. For deterministic independent nonidentically distributed responses, omit calibration unless a local triangular-array score/Hessian theorem is proved with Lindeberg, normalized design-information convergence, no dominating observation, and uniform Taylor remainder conditions. No generic saturated-model chi-square or deviance-residual law. **B:** logistic separation, Poisson overdispersion, identity-link boundary. **Requires:** SME-01; MSF-04/05/07; MSF-15 only for the matching iid random-design route; published matrix differentiation. **Sources:** MIT 18.650 pp. 10–21, 23–33, 40–52; CMU Tibshirani pp. 1–5. Deviance diagnostics source gap remains.

pairs.title: Multivariate normal, Wishart, and Hotelling $T^2$
findings_and_repairs: Corrected the exact Wishart trace statistic degrees of freedom to p(n−1) and separated it from the covariance likelihood-ratio statistic’s asymptotic p(p+1)/2 degrees of freedom.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** multivariate-normal-wishart-hotelling / multivariate-normal-wishart-hotelling-examples. **A:** For iid $X_i\sim N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$, $\Sigma\succ0$, define $\bar X=n^{-1}\sum_iX_i$ and $S=(n-1)^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)(X_i-\bar X)^T$. For $n>p$, prove $\bar X$ and $S$ independent and $(n-1)S\sim W_p(\Sigma,n-1)$, defining the Wishart law as the law of $\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}Z_jZ_j^T$ for iid $Z_j\sim N_p(0,\Sigma)$. Then $T^2=n(\bar X-\mu_0)^TS^{-1}(\bar X-\mu_0)$ satisfies $(n-p)T^2/\{p(n-1)\}\sim F_{p,n-p}$ under $H_0:\mu=\mu_0$. Under $H_0:\Sigma=\Sigma_0$, the distinct exact trace statistic $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_0^{-1}(n-1)S)\sim\chi^2_{p(n-1)}$; the covariance likelihood-ratio statistic has a separate regular fixed-dimensional asymptotic calibration with $p(p+1)/2$ degrees of freedom under MSF-15's matching iid/interior premises. **Proof:** orthogonally decompose the $n$ sample rows into the mean coordinate and $n-1$ residual coordinates. For Hotelling, whiten by $\Sigma^{1/2}$, rotate the mean vector to $e_1$, and use the Schur-complement identity $1/(e_1^TW^{-1}e_1)=g_1^T(I-P_{G_2})g_1$; its independent $\chi^2_{n-p}$ and $\chi^2_p$ factors give the stated $F$ law. Spell out full rank a.s. and covariance conventions in the item proof. **B:** $n\le p$, singular sample covariance, exact/asymptotic distinction. **Requires:** SME-01/03; MSF-04/08/10/15/35 as appropriate; published multivariate-normal and moment clauses (AC inherited). **Sources:** Springer Ch. 3 pp. 1–87 (55–62), Ch. 5 §5.5 pp. 47–66, Ch. 6 §§6.3–6.4 pp. 20–42; Mukherjee Lectures 2–3 cross-check but defer proof parts.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

pairs.title: PCA and eigengap stability
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** principal-components-and-eigenspace-stability / principal-components-and-eigenspace-stability-examples. **A:** Define covariance-PCA as the ordered eigenspaces of $\operatorname{Cov}(X)$, and correlation-PCA as those of the covariance matrix after each coordinate is divided by its positive standard deviation. State the centering/scaling convention. A repeated leading eigenvalue identifies its invariant subspace but not a distinguished unit vector. Locally prove for symmetric $A$, simple leading eigenvalue gap $g=\lambda_1(A)-\lambda_2(A)>0$, symmetric $E$ with $\epsilon=\|E\|_2<g/2$, and leading unit eigenvectors $v,\tilde v$, that $|\lambda_1(A+E)-\lambda_1(A)|\le\epsilon$ and $\sin\angle(v,\tilde v)\le\epsilon/(g-\epsilon)$; the perturbed leading eigenvalue is simple. The proof uses Courant–Fischer and projects the perturbed eigen-equation onto $v^\perp$. For iid $X_i$ with finite fourth moments, prove $\|\hat\Sigma-\Sigma\|_F=O_P(n^{-1/2})$ entrywise by Chebyshev/finite-dimensional norm comparison; an isolated simple leading eigenvalue then gives eigenspace consistency. This is a local bound, not general Davis–Kahan or finite-sample selected-component inference. **B:** tied eigenvalues, sign ambiguity, scale changes and small gaps. **Requires:** SME-01/02; cor-real-spectral-theorem-for-self-adjoint-endomorphisms, thm-courant-fischer-min-max-principle, and published covariance algebra. **Sources:** Springer Ch. 9 pp. 1–43, especially 2–15; Mukherjee Lecture 8 pp. 2–4; perturbation proof local.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

pairs.title: Mixed effects and longitudinal models
findings_and_repairs: Resolved “published Gaussian conditioning” to exact published law/projection/least-squares items; arbitrary-dimensional block-Gaussian conditioning remains a local proof.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** mixed-effects-and-longitudinal-models / mixed-effects-and-longitudinal-models-examples. **A:** For fixed design define $Y=X\beta+Zb+\epsilon$, $Eb=E\epsilon=0$, $\operatorname{Cov}(b)=G$, $\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon)=R$, $b\perp\epsilon$, giving $V=\operatorname{Cov}(Y)=ZGZ^T+R$; Gaussianity is needed for the joint-normal conditional formula, not this covariance identity. With known $V\succ0$ and full-column-rank $X$, define GLS $\hat\beta=(X^TV^{-1}X)^{-1}X^TV^{-1}Y$, prove it is BLUE by whitening, and state $\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\beta)=(X^TV^{-1}X)^{-1}$. For known $\beta,G,R$ under joint Gaussianity, state $E[b\mid Y]=GZ^TV^{-1}(Y-X\beta)$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(b\mid Y)=G-GZ^TV^{-1}ZG$. For unknown fixed effects, define $\hat b=GZ^TV^{-1}(Y-X\hat\beta_{\rm GLS})$ as the BLUP and give $\operatorname{Cov}(b-\hat b)=G-GZ^TV^{-1}ZG+GZ^TV^{-1}X(X^TV^{-1}X)^{-1}X^TV^{-1}ZG$; distinguish this known-$V$ result from empirical BLUP with estimated variance components. Under the Gaussian model, define REML as the likelihood of error contrasts $K^TY$, where $K$ has full row rank, $KX=0$, and rows span $\operatorname{col}(X)^\perp$; their law eliminates $\beta$. Variance components are identifiable iff $\theta\mapsto V(\theta)$ is injective on the stated parameter space. State subject/visit indices and missing-visit/dropout mechanism; covariance equations do not imply ignorability. **B:** random-intercept ICC, aliased slope, informative dropout. **Requires:** SME-01/02; MSF-01/02/04; MSF-03 only for explicit prediction-risk comparisons; published `def-multivariate-normal-law`, `thm-normal-equations-for-best-affine-l2-prediction`, `thm-least-squares-solutions-and-normal-equation`, and `thm-orthogonal-projection-is-the-unique-nearest-point`. Prove the arbitrary-dimensional Gaussian block-conditioning formulas locally by a residual/Schur-complement argument, including the allowed singular latent covariance; `ex-conditional-density-of-a-bivariate-normal-law` is a cross-check only. Carry AC from the Gaussian and L2 suppliers. **Sources:** Duke STA610 Lecture 1 pp. 1–11, Lecture 3 pp. 1–9, Lecture 4 pp. 1–6, Lecture 5 pp. 8–10 (states BLUP, does not prove general matrix result), Lecture 6 pp. 1–16, Lecture 7 pp. 1–21. No Bayesian or computational procedure.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X,Y_1,\dots,Y_n$ be square-integrable real random variables on one
probability space, and write
$$W:=\operatorname{span}\big([1],[Y_1],\dots,[Y_n]\big)\subseteq L^2(\mathbb P),$$
where $[\cdot]$ denotes the almost-everywhere class from
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]].

Then there is a unique class $[Z_*]\in W$ minimizing $\|[X]-[Z]\|_2$ over
$[Z]\in W$. This minimizing class has an affine representative
$Z_*=a_0+\sum_{j=1}^n a_jY_j$, and its coefficients satisfy
$$a_0=\mathbb E[X]-\sum_{j=1}^n a_j\mathbb E[Y_j],$$
$$\sum_{j=1}^n \operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j)a_j=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y_i)\qquad(1\le i\le n).$$

The class $[Z_*]$ is unique. If the covariance matrix
$\Gamma=(\operatorname{Cov}(Y_i,Y_j))_{i,j}$ is singular, the coefficient vector
need not be uniquely determined by the normal equations, but any two solutions
yield the same predictor almost surely.

pairs.title: Finite populations and design probability
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** finite-populations-and-sampling-designs / finite-populations-and-sampling-designs-examples. **A:** Let $U=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be fixed with fixed values $y_i$, target total $T=\sum_Uy_i$ or mean $T/N$, and sample $s\subseteq U$ drawn from a declared probability mass function $p_d(s)$. Define $I_i=1\{i\in s\}$, $\pi_i=P_d(I_i=1)$, $\pi_{ij}=P_d(I_i=I_j=1)$, and design expectation $E_d$ while holding all $y_i$ fixed. For $\pi_i>0$, $\hat T_{HT}=\sum_U I_iy_i/\pi_i$ is design-unbiased. If $\pi_i=0$, two finite populations differing only at that unit induce the same observed-data law but different totals, so no observed-sample estimator is unbiased for every finite population. Distinguish this probability law from a superpopulation model that randomizes the $y_i$. **B:** census, SRSWOR, certainty unit, unobserved unit. **Requires:** SME-01/02; MSF-01/02; published probability law, expectation linearity, and indicator expectation. **Sources:** Shalabh Chs. 1–2 pp. 1–15; Borkowski 6.1–6.2/printed pp. 141–143.

3. $$|\mathbb E[X]|\le\mathbb E[|X|].$$

future_proof_authoring_obligations.scope_and_assumptions_clause_verbatim: **Pages:** finite-populations-and-sampling-designs / finite-populations-and-sampling-designs-examples. **A:** Let $U=\{1,\ldots,N\}$ be fixed with fixed values $y_i$, target total $T=\sum_Uy_i$ or mean $T/N$, and sample $s\subseteq U$ drawn from a declared probability mass function $p_d(s)$. Define $I_i=1\{i\in s\}$, $\pi_i=P_d(I_i=1)$, $\pi_{ij}=P_d(I_i=I_j=1)$, and design expectation $E_d$ while holding all $y_i$ fixed. For $\pi_i>0$, $\hat T_{HT}=\sum_U I_iy_i/\pi_i$ is design-unbiased. If $\pi_i=0$, two finite populations differing only at that unit induce the same observed-data law but different totals, so no observed-sample estimator is unbiased for every finite population. Distinguish this probability law from a superpopulation model that randomizes the $y_i$. **B:** census, SRSWOR, certainty unit, unobserved unit.

pairs.title: HT variance and SRSWOR
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** horvitz-thompson-variance-and-srswor / horvitz-thompson-variance-and-srswor-examples. **A:** Define $\Delta_{ij}=\pi_{ij}-\pi_i\pi_j$. If every $\pi_i>0$, prove $ \operatorname{Var}_d(\hat T_{HT})=\sum_{i,j\in U}\Delta_{ij}y_iy_j/(\pi_i\pi_j)$. The unbiased pair-inclusion estimate $\sum_{i,j\in s}(\Delta_{ij}/\pi_{ij})(y_i/\pi_i)(y_j/\pi_j)$ requires every $\pi_{ij}>0$; zero pair support does not license division or imply variance estimability. For fixed sample size, $\sum_j\Delta_{ij}=0$ yields the Sen–Yates–Grundy identity $-\tfrac12\sum_{i,j}\Delta_{ij}(y_i/\pi_i-y_j/\pi_j)^2$, nonnegative only when $\Delta_{ij}\le0$ for all distinct pairs. For SRSWOR of $n$ from $N>1$, derive $\operatorname{Cov}_d(I_i,I_j)=-n(N-n)/(N^2(N-1))$ for $i\ne j$ and $\operatorname{Var}_d(\bar y)=(1-n/N)S_U^2/n$, where $S_U^2=\sum_U(y_i-\bar y_U)^2/(N-1)$. This design variance does not imply exact normal inference. **B:** zero pair inclusion, census, $n=1$. **Requires:** SME-08; published covariance bilinearity and finite-sum variance. **Sources:** Shalabh Ch. 7 pp. 23–31, Ch. 2 pp. 1–23; Borkowski 6.2 pp. 143–146; Oehlert Ch. 7. Correct Shalabh p.14 sign; exclude Borkowski p.145 PPS arithmetic.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

$$\operatorname{Cov}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}a_iX_i,\sum_{j\in J}b_jY_j\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\sum_{j\in J}a_ib_j\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,Y_j).$$

$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$

pairs.title: Stratification and allocation
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** stratified-sampling-and-allocation / stratified-sampling-and-allocation-examples. **A:** Define a partition $U=\bigsqcup_hU_h$, $N_h=|U_h|$, independent within-stratum SRSWOR of $n_h$ units, and $S_h^2=\sum_{i\in U_h}(y_i-\bar y_h)^2/(N_h-1)$ for noncertainty strata with $N_h>1$. A certainty stratum $n_h=N_h$ contributes zero variance without requiring $S_h^2$. Prove $\hat T_{st}=\sum_hN_h\bar y_{h,s}$ is design-unbiased and $\operatorname{Var}_d(\hat T_{st})=\sum_{h:n_h<N_h}N_h^2(1-n_h/N_h)S_h^2/n_h$. For continuous allocations with fixed $\sum_hn_h=n$, derive $n_h\propto N_hS_h$; with per-unit cost $c_h>0$ and fixed cost budget derive $n_h\propto N_hS_h/\sqrt{c_h}$. These optima assume positive variances in noncertainty strata and no integer, lower-bound, capacity or minimum-sample constraints; handle zero-variance strata and constrained rounding separately. **B:** proportional/disproportionate allocation, zero-variance stratum, rounding. **Requires:** SME-08/09; finite covariance and constrained optimization proof local. **Sources:** Shalabh Ch. 4 complete chapter; JPSM outline is not proof.
pairs.exact_supplier_clause: SME-08/09; finite covariance and constrained optimization proof local.

findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** cluster-and-two-stage-sampling / cluster-and-two-stage-sampling-examples. **A:** Define a primary sampling unit (PSU), secondary sampling unit (SSU), cluster total and the exact first/second-stage sample laws. For SRSWOR of $m$ clusters from $M$, prove the total estimator $M$ times the sample mean of cluster totals has variance $M^2(1-m/M)S_T^2/m$. In two-stage sampling define the expansion estimator and derive its variance by conditioning on the first-stage sample: variance of true PSU totals plus expected within-PSU sampling variance, with the stage-specific inclusion probabilities stated. Separately, for equal cluster size $m_c$, equal marginal variance, common within-cluster correlation $\rho$, and negligible FPC, derive $DEFF=\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_{\rm cluster})/\operatorname{Var}(\bar Y_{\rm element\ SRS})=1+(m_c-1)\rho$. $\rho=0$ means no ICC inflation, not zero sampling error. Do not transfer this formula to unequal sizes/weights or nonexchangeable covariance. **B:** village/field subsampling and unequal cluster shortcut failure. **Requires:** SME-08; published covariance algebra and conditional-variance decomposition. **Sources:** Shalabh Chs. 9–10 complete; Holmes–Huber Ch.13. Correct Shalabh Ch.9 p.7 wording.

pairs.title: Assignment randomization and sharp-null tests
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** randomized-treatment-assignment-and-sharp-null-tests / randomized-treatment-assignment-and-sharp-null-tests-examples. **A:** Define finite experimental units $i=1,\ldots,N$, assignment space $\mathcal Z$ with known probabilities $p(z)$, fixed potential-outcome schedule $Y_i(z)$, observed outcome $Y_i(Z)$, and statistic $T(z,Y(z))$. Under the Fisher sharp null $Y_i(z)=Y_i(z')$ for every $i,z,z'$, all assignment outcomes are imputable. For a predeclared upper-tail ordering, $p_{\rm rand}=\sum_{z\in\mathcal Z}p(z)1\{T(z)\ge T(Z_{\rm obs})\}$ is superuniform under the actual assignment law; $p^+=P_d(T>T_{\rm obs})+U P_d(T=T_{\rm obs})$, with independent $U\sim U(0,1)$, is uniform. State the statistic and two-sided ordering explicitly. The sharp null is not the weak null of zero average effect; random assignment supplies no Gaussian error law. **Proof:** enumerate the finite weighted orbit and use the discrete probability integral transform; for randomized ties, partition the unit interval by the statistic's atom masses. **B:** sharp versus average null, unequal assignment probabilities and ties. **Requires:** SME-01; MSF-02/08; finite-sum probability. This is a treatment-assignment theorem, not the generic finite-group orbit interface of MSF-11. **Sources:** Oehlert Ch.13; Holmes–Huber Ch.13; local design proof.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Under $Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+\beta_j+\epsilon_{ij}$ and independent mean-zero Gaussian equal-variance errors, derive the RCBD treatment contrast/F law separately; with one observation per block-treatment cell, interaction cannot be separated from residual error. Define a Latin square as a treatment-by-row-by-column allocation with each treatment once in each row and column, and state its restricted randomization law separately from an RCBD. **B:** missing treatment, treatment-by-block interaction, Latin-square allocation. **Requires:** SME-12; MSF-02; covariance algebra and MSF-35 only for exact Gaussian F inference. **Sources:** Oehlert Ch.13; NIST §5.3.3.2 pp.1303–1306; Holmes–Huber 13.4.4. audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim: Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

pairs.title: Full factorials
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** full-factorial-contrasts-and-interactions / full-factorial-contrasts-and-interactions-examples. **A:** For one observation at each of all $2^k$ runs $x\in\{-1,+1\}^k$, define effect column $x_A=\prod_{j\in A}x_j$ for subset $A\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$, with $x_\varnothing=1$. Prove $2^{-k}X^TX=I$ by sign cancellation over $A\triangle B$. In $Y=X\beta+\epsilon$, define $\hat\beta_A=2^{-k}\sum_xx_AY_x$; the usual factorial effect for nonempty $A$ is $2\hat\beta_A$. Under independent errors with common variance $\sigma^2$, derive $\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_A)=\sigma^2/2^k$ and the corresponding effect variance. Replication changes this by its declared run count. Orthogonality is a design-matrix fact, not additivity, zero interaction, or a physical mechanism. **B:** interaction, scale dependence, unbalanced loss. **Requires:** SME-12; finite-dimensional inner-product and covariance algebra. **Sources:** Oehlert Ch.8; NIST §5.3.3.3 pp.1320–1328.

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$

pairs.title: Fractional factorial aliases and foldover
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** fractional-factorial-aliasing-and-foldover / fractional-factorial-aliasing-and-foldover-examples. **A:** Define a regular $2^{k-p}$ fraction by $p$ independent generators and its defining subgroup $H$; effects $A$ and $B$ are aliased exactly when their sign columns agree on the fraction, equivalently $AB\in H$. Define the defining relation and resolution as the shortest nonidentity word in $H$. Equal alias columns cannot have separately estimated coefficients absent further runs or a sparsity/hierarchy assumption. For a complete mirror foldover that reverses all factor signs, prove a word of order $r$ changes sign by $(-1)^r$; opposite-parity aliases separate, same-parity members may remain aliased. A partial foldover separates only the targeted columns and must list residual aliases. **B:** $I=ABC$ aliases and full/partial foldover. **Requires:** SME-14; sign-product linear algebra. **Sources:** Oehlert Chs.15,18; NIST §5.3.3.4.1–.4 pp.1333–1347 and 5.3.3.8 pp.1382–1389.

pairs.title: Response surfaces and optimal design
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** response-surfaces-and-optimal-design / response-surfaces-and-optimal-design-examples. **A:** Define a response surface as a local polynomial approximation on a declared factor region; for a second-order model $m(x)=\beta_0+x^T\beta+x^TBx$ with symmetric nonsingular $B$, derive stationary point $x_0=-\tfrac12B^{-1}\beta$ and classify it by the eigenvalue signs of $B$, only within the fitted model/region. Define a central composite design by factorial/fractional-factorial, axial and center runs. For $y=f(x)^T\beta+\epsilon$ with independent homoscedastic variance $\sigma^2$, an approximate design is weights $\xi_x\ge0,\sum_x\xi_x=1$ on a finite candidate set, $M(\xi)=\sum_x\xi_xf(x)f(x)^T$. Define D-optimality as maximizing $\log\det M$, A-optimality as minimizing $\operatorname{tr}(M^{-1})$, E-optimality as maximizing $\lambda_{\min}(M)$, and c-optimality as minimizing $c^TM^{-1}c$, on nonsingular designs (with estimability specified for singular cases). State these are different model/candidate-dependent goals. Prove the D-equivalence theorem: a nonsingular $\xi^*$ is D-optimal iff $f(x)^TM(\xi^*)^{-1}f(x)\le p$ for every candidate and equality holds on its support; necessity uses the logdet directional derivative and sufficiency concavity, with support equality by averaging to $p$. Exact integer-run optimality is a separate finite design problem. **B:** saddle, approximate versus exact design. **Requires:** SME-14/15; published determinant differential and local proof of logdet concavity. **Sources:** Oehlert Ch. 19 §§19.1–19.7; Boyd–Vandenberghe §§3.1.5 and 7.5 for logdet concavity/equivalence proof; NIST §§5.3.3.6–.9 pp. 1356–1392 supports examples only.
pairs.exact_supplier_clause: SME-14/15; published determinant differential and local proof of logdet concavity.

pairs.title: Power and sample size
findings_and_repairs: Specified positive integer sample-size domain, alpha/beta domain, and the least-n formula for all open-unit-interval alpha/beta values.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** power-and-sample-size-planning / power-and-sample-size-planning-examples. **A:** Define test size $\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}P_\theta(\text{reject})$, power $P_{\theta_1}(\text{reject})$, type-II error $1-$power, target effect/precision, allocation, sidedness and feasible integer sample sizes. The planning procedure takes those inputs plus a specified sampling law/test, computes its power at each candidate positive integer size $n\in\mathbb N_{\ge1}$ and outputs the least feasible $n$ attaining the target (or reports none); it is not a universal design guarantee. For $X_i\stackrel{iid}{\sim}N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with known $\sigma>0$ and $\alpha,\beta\in(0,1)$, testing $H_0:\mu\le\mu_0$ against $\mu_1=\mu_0+\delta$, $\delta>0$, by $Z>\Phi^{-1}(1-\alpha)$, derive power $\Phi(\delta\sqrt n/\sigma-z_{1-\alpha})$ and least integer $n\ge1$ as $\max\{1,\lceil(\sigma/\delta)^2\max\{0,z_{1-\alpha}+z_{1-\beta}\}^2\rceil\}$. If the z-quantile sum is nonpositive, every positive $n$ meets the stated target. Two-sided power includes both tails and must be computed from its stated rejection region. Unknown-$\sigma$ $t$ designs and other sampling laws require separate exact/noncentral derivations. **B:** one/two-sided and variance/effect sensitivity. **Requires:** SME-08/12; MSF-08 power definition; normal-law and quantile conventions. **Sources:** Oehlert Ch.7; NIST §7.2.2.2 pp.2019–2021.

audited_existing_suppliers.reusable_clause_exact: Scalar normal laws and density normalization; the normal-law definition is homed here rather than on the CLT page. Positive variance is required for exact Student/F denominators.
audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

pairs.title: Biological and technical replication
findings_and_repairs: Conditioned the displayed variance on fixed treatment contributions and recorded the additional variance needed if treatment varies randomly across units.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** biological-and-technical-replication / biological-and-technical-replication-examples. **A:** Define biological units as the independent units sampled/randomized at the intended level of generalization and technical replicates as repeated measurements of the same material/unit. Conditional on fixed treatment effects $\tau_i$ (or on a common assigned treatment level), under $Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+b_i+\epsilon_{ij}$ with independent biological effects $b_i$ of variance $\sigma_b^2$ and independent technical errors $\epsilon_{ij}$ of variance $\sigma_e^2$, derive variance of the mean over $n$ independent biological units and $m$ measurements each: $\sigma_b^2/n+\sigma_e^2/(nm)$. If treatment contributions are random across units, their variance must be added under the stated assignment law. If treatment is assigned to a cage, litter, plot or batch, that assignment cluster is the randomized replicate. Technical repeats reduce the measurement component, not the number of independent biological units. **B:** five assays on one animal versus one assay on five animals. **Requires:** SME-01/07; published covariance algebra. **Sources:** Oehlert Ch.1 p.6; Holmes–Huber 13.3.2,13.4.2,13.4.5.
pairs.exact_supplier_clause: SME-01/07; published covariance algebra.

audited_existing_suppliers.reusable_clause_exact: Measurable observations/laws, expectation and indicator linearity, finite moments/covariance and affine L2 projection. Predictor class is unique even if coefficients are not. No sampling-design or model-specific inference theorem.
audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X,Y$ be square-integrable real random variables on one probability space.
Then
$$\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb E[X^2]-\mathbb E[X]^2,$$
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\mathbb E[XY]-\mathbb E[X]\mathbb E[Y].$$
Moreover, covariance is symmetric and bilinear on finite linear combinations.
On finite full-power-set probability spaces these formulas reduce to the
published finite identities.

future_proof_authoring_obligations.scope_and_assumptions_clause_verbatim: **Pages:** biological-and-technical-replication / biological-and-technical-replication-examples. **A:** Define biological units as the independent units sampled/randomized at the intended level of generalization and technical replicates as repeated measurements of the same material/unit. Conditional on fixed treatment effects $\tau_i$ (or on a common assigned treatment level), under $Y_{ij}=\mu+\tau_i+b_i+\epsilon_{ij}$ with independent biological effects $b_i$ of variance $\sigma_b^2$ and independent technical errors $\epsilon_{ij}$ of variance $\sigma_e^2$, derive variance of the mean over $n$ independent biological units and $m$ measurements each: $\sigma_b^2/n+\sigma_e^2/(nm)$. If treatment contributions are random across units, their variance must be added under the stated assignment law. If treatment is assigned to a cage, litter, plot or batch, that assignment cluster is the randomized replicate. Technical repeats reduce the measurement component, not the number of independent biological units. **B:** five assays on one animal versus one assay on five animals.

findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** potential-outcomes-and-causal-identification / potential-outcomes-and-causal-identification-examples. **A:** Define treatment version $a$, potential outcome $Y^a$, observed outcome $Y=Y^A$ under consistency, target-population ATE $E(Y^1-Y^0)$ and CATE $E(Y^1-Y^0\mid L)$, conditional exchangeability $(Y^a:a\in\mathcal A)\perp A\mid L$, and positivity. The displayed point-treatment theorem is for discrete $A$ with $P(A=a)>0$ and $P(A=a\mid L)>0$ a.s. under the target $L$-law; require integrable potential outcomes. For discrete $L$, prove $E[Y^a]=\sum_l E[Y\mid A=a,L=l]P(L=l)$; state the standard-Borel RCD/integral version over $L$. For continuous $A$, RCDs identify conditional laws only for $P_A$-almost every treatment value; do not claim pointwise identification at a null value $a$ without a specified version/continuity/smoothness premise and a separate proof. Identification is constancy of the target over full-data laws compatible with the observed law and assumptions; it is not empirical plausibility. Exchangeability is generally untestable and positivity failure leaves target strata unsupported. **B:** randomized, binary confounding, positivity failure. **Requires:** MSF-01; existing def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra, conditional expectation, and RCD/disintegration items (AC inherited by conditional expectation/RCD existence). **Sources:** H&R Ch.1 1.1–1.5 and Ch.3 3.1–3.6 printed pp.3–12,27–45; Kang strong-ignorability review.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

pairs.title: SCM, DAGs, adjustment
findings_and_repairs: Separated causal Markov/d-separation/faithfulness interfaces from Markov-equivalence/CPDAG results and corrected full-graph adjustment/support clauses.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** structural-causal-models-dags-and-adjustment / structural-causal-models-dags-and-adjustment-examples. **A:** Define a recursive SCM on a finite DAG $G=(V,E)$ with observed and latent endogenous nodes: $X_j=f_j(X_{\operatorname{pa}(j)},U_j)$, measurable structural functions, and an explicit exogenous law. In the Markovian expanded model require mutually independent $U_j$; state the full-joint law as a topological product of probability kernels, then obtain the observed law by marginalizing latent nodes. An observed-only DAG factorization is claimed only under causal sufficiency or the stated latent structure. Define $do(X_k=a)$ by replacing only its structural equation. On the full DAG, call an internal path node a collider when both adjacent arrows point into it, and a noncollider otherwise; let $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ contain $v$ and all its directed descendants. A path is active given $C$ iff every noncollider lies outside $C$ and every collider has a member of $\operatorname{De}^+(v)$ in $C$; d-separation means no active path joins the queried sets. State the global Markov implication (full DAG factorization implies d-separation conditional independence); define faithfulness separately as its converse for the specified law. No Markov-equivalence or skeleton/unshielded-collider characterization is claimed here. For displayed pointwise adjustment formulas, restrict $A$ to discrete/atomic values of positive probability. For backdoor adjustment, evaluate paths in the full DAG after deleting arrows out of $A$; require $L$ contain no descendants of $A$, d-separate $A,Y$, and $P(A=a\mid L)>0$ a.s. on target support; then $P(Y\mid do(A=a))=\int P(Y\mid A=a,L=l)P_L(dl)$. For front-door, use the full graph including latent nodes and require (i) $M$ intercepts all directed $A\to Y$ paths, (ii) no open backdoor path $A$-$M$, and (iii) all backdoor paths $M$-$Y$ are blocked by $A$. Require $P(A=a)>0$ and the support conditions for nested conditional laws; in the discrete case, for each $m$ with $P(M=m\mid A=a)>0$, require $P(A=a'\mid M=m)>0$ for every $a'$ with $P(A=a')>0$. Prove the front-door functional $\int P(dm\mid A=a)\int E(Y\mid M=m,A=a')P_A(da')$. For continuous $A$, regular conditional kernels identify these formulas only for $P_A$-almost every $a$; pointwise intervention effects at a null value require a specified version plus continuity/smoothness assumptions and a separate proof. These are sufficient criteria only. **Proof:** derive the full-joint kernel factorization from independent exogenous variables in topological order; marginalize latent nodes; prove the global Markov implication by local factorization/elimination; derive adjustment formulas by intervention factorization. **B:** confounder/mediator/collider and two SCMs with the same observed law but different intervention laws. **Interfaces:** def-recursive-structural-causal-model-and-dag; def-d-separation-in-a-dag; thm-dag-factorization-implies-d-separation-conditional-independence; def-faithfulness-of-a-dag-model; thm-backdoor-adjustment-sufficiency; thm-frontdoor-adjustment-sufficiency. **Requires:** SME-19; MSF-01; existing def-conditional-independence-given-a-sigma-algebra (published, AC); probability-kernel and conditional-law items. **Sources:** Pearl 3.1–3.3 PDF pp.24–36/journal pp.119–131; H&R Chs.6–7 pp.75–107. The local proofs must not rely on faithfulness to infer missing arrows or on an unreviewed Markov-equivalence theorem.

audited_existing_suppliers.reusable_clause_exact: Product laws for independent observations/subjects; pairwise independence is not mutual independence.
audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** standardization-and-ipw-identification / standardization-and-ipw-identification-examples. **A:** Under SME-19's discrete/atomic treatment scope, for $e_a(L)=P(A=a\mid L)>0$ a.s. and integrable $Y^a$, define $\int E(Y\mid A=a,L=l)\,P_L(dl)$ and prove it equals $E[Y^a]$. Also prove $E[1\{A=a\}Y/e_a(L)]=E[Y^a]$ by conditioning on $L$, consistency and exchangeability. These are population identities for known true probabilities; they imply no finite-sample stability, estimated-weight consistency, or validity after weight truncation. For continuous $A$, replace the indicator/probability by a density or another declared intervention functional; an RCD formula is only a.e. in $a$ unless extra version/regularity conditions and proof are supplied. **B:** correct adjustment, extreme weights, truncation changing target. **Requires:** SME-19; MSF-01; existing conditional-expectation tower and indicator identities (AC for the conditional-expectation route). **Sources:** H&R Ch.2 Technical Points 2.2–2.3 and Ch.3 pp.27–45.

pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** mediation-effects-and-identification / mediation-effects-and-identification-examples. **A:** Define $M(a)$ and $Y(a,m)$, controlled direct effect $E[Y(a,m)-Y(a',m)]$, natural direct effect $E[Y(a,M(a'))-Y(a',M(a'))]$, and natural indirect effect $E[Y(a,M(a))-Y(a,M(a'))]$, naming both reference levels. The standard natural-effect formula requires consistency, treatment and mediator positivity, no unmeasured treatment–outcome and mediator–outcome confounding, no treatment-induced mediator–outcome confounder, and an explicit cross-world restriction such as NPSEM-IE; FFRCISTG alone does not imply that restriction. State the exact conditional-law formula and identify its target before claiming identification. Separable/interventionist effects require meaningful component interventions and dismissible-component restrictions and define different targets. No regression coefficient alone identifies these effects. **B:** mediator confounding, treatment-induced confounding, and compatible observed laws with different cross-world effects. **Requires:** SME-19/20; MSF-01. **Sources:** H&R Ch.23 23.1–23.4/Technical Points pp.323–331; Pearl 5.1 pp.39–41.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

pairs.title: Interference and exposure mappings
findings_and_repairs: Specified Hudgens–Halloran’s two-stage randomization, group-average estimands/estimators, and stratified-interference boundary after reading the cited sections.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** interference-exposure-mappings-and-design-based-effects / interference-exposure-mappings-and-design-based-effects-examples. **A:** Define fixed finite-population outcomes $Y_{ij}(\mathbf z_i)$, assignment vector $\mathbf Z_i$, and partial interference as invariance to assignments outside group $i$. An exposure mapping $D_{ij}=f_{ij}(\mathbf Z_i)$ is sufficient only if $Y_{ij}(\mathbf z_i)=Y_{ij}(d)$ whenever $f_{ij}(\mathbf z_i)=d$. With $\pi_{ij}(d)=P_d(D_{ij}(\mathbf Z_i)=d)>0$, prove the design-unbiased exposure mean $N^{-1}\sum_{ij}Y_{ij}(d)$ is estimated by $N^{-1}\sum_{ij}1\{D_{ij}=d\}Y_{ij}/\pi_{ij}(d)$. For the two-stage result, define $N>1$ groups with fixed sizes $n_i$, fixed outcomes, and strategies $\psi,\phi$. First choose exactly $C\in\{1,\ldots,N-1\}$ groups uniformly for $\psi$; second, within a group assigned strategy $s$, choose a fixed $K_i^s\in\{1,\ldots,n_i-1\}$ units uniformly for treatment. Define $\bar Y_i(z;\psi)=n_i^{-1}\sum_jE_\psi[Y_{ij}(\mathbf Z_i)\mid Z_{ij}=z]$, $\bar Y(z;\psi)=N^{-1}\sum_i\bar Y_i(z;\psi)$, and $\bar Y(\psi)=N^{-1}\sum_i n_i^{-1}\sum_jE_\psi[Y_{ij}(\mathbf Z_i)]$. Define $DE(\psi)=\bar Y(0;\psi)-\bar Y(1;\psi)$, $IE(\phi,\psi)=\bar Y(0;\phi)-\bar Y(0;\psi)$, $TE(\phi,\psi)=\bar Y(0;\phi)-\bar Y(1;\psi)$, and $OE(\phi,\psi)=\bar Y(\phi)-\bar Y(\psi)$. Give the source estimators explicitly: $\hat{\bar Y}_i(z;\psi)=\sum_jY_{ij}(\mathbf Z_i)1\{Z_{ij}=z\}/\sum_j1\{Z_{ij}=z\}$, $\hat{\bar Y}(z;\psi)=\sum_i\hat{\bar Y}_i(z;\psi)1\{S_i=\psi\}/\sum_i1\{S_i=\psi\}$, $\hat{\bar Y}_i(\psi)=n_i^{-1}\sum_jY_{ij}(\mathbf Z_i)$, and $\hat{\bar Y}(\psi)=\sum_i\hat{\bar Y}_i(\psi)1\{S_i=\psi\}/\sum_i1\{S_i=\psi\}$; strategy contrasts estimate the four displayed effects. Prove unbiasedness by conditioning first on group strategy and then the uniform within-group allocation. Source variance estimators require stratified interference (outcomes are invariant to which other units receive treatment conditional on their count); their expectation equals the target variance plus a nonnegative between-unit treatment-effect heterogeneity term, so equality requires additive effects. **B:** wrong exposure map, cross-group contamination and nonadditive spillover violating the variance premise. **Requires:** SME-12; MSF-01/02; explicit finite assignment law. **Sources:** Hudgens–Halloran §§2–4 Thms.1–3/Appendix A.1–A.9; Aronow–Samii §§3–4 Lemma 4.1/Prop.4.2 and App. A.2/A.4, PDF pp.4–11 and 1927–2021 lines.

Let $X,Y$ be integrable real or complex random variables on one probability

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** missingness-mechanisms-and-identification / missingness-mechanisms-and-identification-examples. **A:** Define full data $W$, observation-pattern variable $R$, and observed components $W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$. MCAR means $P(R=r\mid W=w)$ is constant in $w$; MAR means for each pattern $r$, $P(R=r\mid W=w)$ depends on $w$ only through $W_{\mathrm{obs}}(r)$; MNAR is the complement relative to this declared partition. For a dominated full-data model $p_\theta(w)$ and response model $g_\psi(r\mid w)$, state product parameter space and factorization; under MAR and parameter distinctness, prove the response factor may be omitted from likelihood inference for $\theta$, but not for every target. For binary $Y$ and response indicator $R$, set $a=P(R=1)$, $b=P(R=1,Y=1)$; under unrestricted MNAR the compatible full mean is exactly $[b,b+1-a]$, while the observed response rate and success mass remain fixed. Death may make a target undefined rather than merely unobserved. **B:** MCAR/MAR/MNAR mechanisms, two full-data laws with the same observed law, and competing death. **Requires:** MSF-01/04; existing RCD/disintegration and dominated-likelihood clauses (AC for RCD). **Sources:** H&R Ch. 8 §§8.1–8.6 and Technical Points 8.1–8.2, printed pp. 109–123, §12.6 pp. 172–173; NRC Ch. 4 pp. 47–58, 70–77 and complete Ch. 5 pp. 83–106; Mao Ch. 1 §§1.1–1.7.

pairs.title: Missingness weights and sensitivity
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** missing-data-weighting-and-sensitivity / missing-data-weighting-and-sensitivity-examples. **A:** Define $R\in\{0,1\}$, fully observed $X$, response probability $\pi(X)=P(R=1\mid X)$, and MAR $Y\perp R\mid X$. If $\pi(X)>0$ a.s. on the target support and $E|Y|<\infty$, prove $E[RY/\pi(X)]=E[Y]$ by conditioning on $X$. findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** measurement-error-and-misclassification / measurement-error-and-misclassification-examples. **A:** Define latent $X$, measured $W$, classical error $W=X+U$, Berkson error $X=W+U$, and categorical misclassification through $P(W=w\mid X=x)$. Call an error nondifferential only relative to named variables, e.g. $W\perp Y\mid X,Z$; this label alone implies no direction of bias. In $Y=\alpha+\beta X+\epsilon$, with centered $X,U,\epsilon$, $U\perp(X,\epsilon)$, $\epsilon\perp X$, finite second moments and $\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(U)>0$, derive the naive slope $\operatorname{Cov}(Y,W)/\operatorname{Var}(W)=\beta\operatorname{Var}(X)/\{\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(U)\}$. State distinct assumptions before any Berkson slope claim. Validation, replicate or known-error-law correction requires its own design/model; the observed $W$-law alone generally does not identify the latent/error variance split. **B:** classical/Berkson, differential misclassification and unidentified latent variance split. **Requires:** MSF-01; MSF-04 only for a stated error likelihood; published covariance identities. **Sources:** H&R Ch. 9 §§9.1–9.6, printed pp. 125–135; Keogh et al. STRATOS §§1–4.3.5, full text lines 104–373.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

pairs.title: Event observation, censoring, truncation
findings_and_repairs: Pair contract reviewed; exact claims, prerequisites, source ranges and proof obligations are transcribed below.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** event-time-censoring-and-truncation / event-time-censoring-and-truncation-examples. **A:** Define event time $T$, censoring time $C$, right-censored observation $U=\min(T,C)$, and $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$; define left censoring, interval censoring $\{L<T\le R\}$, current status at inspection $C$, and left/right truncation as inclusion conditional on $T>L$ or $T<R$, respectively. For a continuous event-time law with density $f(t\mid z)$, survival $S(t\mid z)=P(T>t\mid z)$, and $T\perp C\mid Z$, derive event contribution $f(U\mid Z)^\delta S(U\mid Z)^{1-\delta}$ up to censoring-only factors. Interval observation contributes $F(R\mid Z)-F(L\mid Z)$ only for fixed or noninformative inspection endpoints; current-status $\delta=1\{T\le C\}$ contributes $F(C\mid Z)^\delta S(C\mid Z)^{1-\delta}$ under the same observation-scheme premise. For delayed entry $L$, require entry independent of $T$ conditional on stated covariates and condition the event likelihood on $T>L$, giving denominator $S(L\mid Z)$. Define left/right-truncation selection explicitly; do not reuse the censoring likelihood for a truncated sample. Informative censoring/inspection/entry needs a different model. **B:** censoring/truncation, delayed entry, informative dropout. **Requires:** SME-01; MSF-01/04; published Lebesgue–Stieltjes correspondence (Countable Choice) for distribution/atom clauses. **Sources:** Yu pp.1–11; Stanford Unit 2 pp.1–4; Slud Maryland handout pp.1–2.
pairs.exact_supplier_clause: SME-01; MSF-01/04; published Lebesgue–Stieltjes correspondence (Countable Choice) for distribution/atom clauses.

audited_existing_suppliers.reusable_clause_exact: Distribution/measure dictionary and arbitrary-set counting measure; not random locally finite counting measures or Palm laws.
audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Let $X$ be a set and let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]). A **measure** on $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function

$$\mu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow[0,+\infty]\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$$

such that:

1. $\mu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$,
   $$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k),$$
   where the right side is the nonnegative extended sum of [[def-nonnegative-extended-series]].

The second condition is **countable additivity**. It begins at index $0$ and includes the case in which some term or the total sum is $+\infty$.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let
$F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing and right-continuous, and let
$\mu_F$ be its Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure. Then for every $a < b$,

$$\mu_F((a,b)) = F(b^-) - F(a),$$

$$\mu_F([a,b]) = F(b) - F(a^-),$$

$$\mu_F([a,b)) = F(b^-) - F(a^-),$$

and

$$\mu_F(\{a\}) = F(a) - F(a^-).$$

Consequently $a$ is an atom of $\mu_F$ in the sense of
[[def-atom-of-a-measure-on-r]] if and only if $F(a) > F(a^-)$, and the set of
atoms of $\mu_F$ is at most countable.

audited_existing_suppliers.current_item_clause_excerpt_verbatim:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $\mu$ be a Borel measure on
$\mathbb{R}$ finite on compact sets, and let
$F_\mu$ be its normalized distribution function from
[[def-distribution-function-of-a-borel-measure-on-r]]. Then:

1. $F_\mu$ is nondecreasing and right-continuous;
2. for every $a < b$,

   $$F_\mu(b) - F_\mu(a) = \mu((a,b]);$$

3. the Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure attached to $F_\mu$ is exactly $\mu$.

Conversely, if $F,G : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ are nondecreasing and
right-continuous, then $\mu_F = \mu_G$ if and only if $F-G$ is constant on
$\mathbb{R}$.

pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** parametric-survival-and-reliability / parametric-survival-and-reliability-examples. **A:** Define $S(t)=P(T>t)$, density hazard $\lambda(t)=f(t)/S(t)$ where $S(t)>0$, and cumulative hazard $\Lambda(t)=\int_0^t\lambda(u)\,du$. If $T$ is absolutely continuous and $S(0)=1$, prove $S(t)=e^{-\Lambda(t)}$; state the separate product/jump relation for atoms. Define $T\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$ by $S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$, and Weibull(shape $k>0$, scale $\eta>0$) by $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$. For iid $T_i\sim\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda)$, $U_i=\min(T_i,C_i)$, $\delta_i=1\{T_i\le C_i\}$, and censoring independent of event times with a parameter-distinct censor law, derive likelihood in $\lambda$ proportional to $\lambda^d e^{-\lambda\sum_iU_i}$, $d=\sum_i\delta_i$. If $d>0$ and total exposure is positive, $\hat\lambda=d/\sum_iU_i$; if $d=0$, the likelihood supremum is at $\lambda\downarrow0$, attained only if the parameter space includes the boundary $0$. Repairable-system recurrent failure counts are not a single-lifetime survival model. **B:** constant/Weibull hazard and censored exposure. **Requires:** SME-28; MSF-01/04; published CDF/measure correspondence (Countable Choice). **Sources:** NIST reliability Ch.8 pp.4–19,155–163; Stanford Unit 2 pp.1–7; Yu pp.1–11.

pairs.title: Counting-process compensators, integrals, brackets
findings_and_repairs: Added finite-horizon expected compensator integrability E[A_T]<∞ and local square-integrable martingale/bracket/isometry obligations.
pairs.proposal_text_verbatim: **Pages:** counting-process-compensators-and-integrals / counting-process-compensators-and-integrals-examples. **A, new earlier Cat-2 supplier:** On a finite horizon $[0,T]$, define a simple unit-jump counting process $N$, filtration, predictable $Y$, nonnegative predictable intensity $\lambda$, and continuous increasing $A_t=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds$ with $A_0=0$ and $E[A_T]<\infty$. The model contract is that $M=N-A$ is a square-integrable martingale; do not claim a general compensator-existence theorem from a displayed intensity. Prove $\langle M\rangle=A$, $[M]=N$, and for bounded predictable step $H$, $\int_0^tH_s\,dM_s$ is a square-integrable martingale with $E(\int_0^TH\,dM)^2=E\int_0^TH_s^2\,dA_s$; extend only to predictable $H$ with $E\int H^2dA<\infty$ by $L^2$ completion.
